title: 5...Bg4, pinning the knight
intro:
Black develops with a threat instead of a pawn move. The bishop on g4 pins the knight against the queen and offers a trade that would ruin White's kingside if White took it back the wrong way.

## What the pin is worth

Not much, as long as White answers it properly. The knight on f3 is not doing anything urgent, and the pin is only a nuisance while the queen sits on d1. What the bishop is really after is the trade on f3: if White ever recaptures with the g-pawn, the four healthy kingside pawns become three and a doubled pair, and the whole reason for playing the Exchange goes with them.

## Your answer

6.h3, asking the bishop what it intends. Then whatever it does, recapture on f3 with the QUEEN if the trade comes.

Black has three tries. 6...h5 is the critical one and the only one with teeth: Black offers the bishop and threatens to open the h-file. Do not take it. 7.d3 develops and leaves Black to prove the sacrifice, which the engine says is nothing. 6...Bxf3 7.Qxf3 gives White the two knights against two bishops in a position with no open lines, which is a fair trade for White here. 6...Bh5 walks into 7.g4, and it also sets the trap below.

## The trap that decides the chapter

After 6...Bh5 the knight on f3 is still pinned, and taking on e5 is losing: 7.Nxe5?? Bxd1 and the bishop that has been staring down the diagonal since move five takes the queen. Look at the whole diagonal before capturing, every time.

## Typical mistakes at this level

Taking the bishop on g4 after ...h5. Recapturing on f3 with the g-pawn. Taking on e5 while the diagonal to d1 is open. And playing h3 and then g4 without noticing that the king is being opened up for nothing.

children.note: Ask it back. The bishop has to say whether it means the sacrifice, the trade or a retreat.

mistakes.note: Solid, and it leaves the pin in place for as long as Black wants it.
Playable and slow. The rook on e1 does nothing while Black's pawn sits on e5.

children.note: The critical answer. Black offers the bishop to open the h-file.
Develop and decline. The bishop on g4 is not going anywhere and the h-pawn has weakened Black more than White.

mistakes.note: The knight on f3 then cannot move, because ...Qh4 mates on h1 down the file Black has just opened. 8.Ne1 Qh4 is mate in a few, and even the best 8.Re1 gxf3 9.Qxf3 leaves White level on material with a shattered king.
It opens the position with Black's pieces aimed at the king. Finish developing first.

The knight heads for c4, where it hits e5 and b6 and cannot be traded by a bishop.

mistakes.note: Also playable, and it walks into ...Bxf3 followed by ...Qxb2 ideas. Bring the knight out first.

The knight arrives with a hit on the bishop.

mistakes.note: Still losing, and for the same reason: the file is open and the knight on f3 is what holds h1 together.

children.note: Black trades before the knight settles.

children.plan: Trade queens on f3 or f6 if Black offers, put the bishop on e3 and a rook on d1, and only then start the kingside pawns.
children.note: With the queen, always.

With the queen. The g-pawn stays where it is, and so does the majority.

mistakes.note: It doubles the pawns on the wing this whole opening exists to exploit, and opens the king for nothing. The queen recapture is not a preference, it is the point.

Sidestep and hit e5 and g7. The queen is better placed than Black's.

Quiet and correct. The bishop comes to e3 or g5 next.

Keeping the pin and inviting the pawn forward.
Take the space. The bishop has to go to g6 where it is out of play.

mistakes.note: The diagonal from h5 to d1 has been open since move five: 7...Bxd1, and after the recapture White has given the queen for a bishop and a pawn. Look down the whole diagonal before taking.

Now it works, because the queen is no longer at the end of that diagonal. A clean pawn.

Take, and the doubled pawns get worse.
